utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: The party seeking protective measures for a witness must demonstrate an objectively grounded risk to the security or welfare of the witness or the witness's family, should it become known that the witness has given evidence before the Tribunal. However, where an application for protective measures concerns a sexual assault victim, a long line of authority provides that the identity of such a victim will be protected based on considerations of privacy, if that victim so requests even in the absence of any concerns about the witness's security. In the present case, Witness 61 testified about being the victim of rape. The Chamber, therefore, granted the requested protective measures on the basis of the special consideration applied to persons testifying about their personal experience of sexual violence. This concludes the reasons for the Trial Chamber's decision on protective measures for Witness 61. The next decision to be delivered is this Chamber's decision on the Prosecution's motion seeking an amendment to Idriz Balaj's pre-trial brief. During cross-examination of Witness 19 on the 16th of March, 2007, counsel for Idriz Balaj asked about a murder committed by a relative of the witness many years prior to the indictment period. Counsel suggested that what later happened to this relative during the indictment period might have been the result of a personal revenge or blood feud for this murder. The Prosecution objected to the questioning as not having a sufficient basis and being irrelevant. The Chamber overruled the objection. On the 30th of March, 2007, the Prosecution filed a motion seeking an amendment to Idriz Balaj's pre-trial brief. The Prosecution argued that the fact that the reference to blood feud was made for the first time during the cross-examination of Witness 19 and not mentioned in the pre-trial brief constituted a breach of Rule 65 ter (F). In the Prosecution's understanding, Balaj intended to use the same defence in cross-examination of other witnesses as well. The Prosecution argued that by not being informed in general terms that the issue of a blood feud would be raised in cross-examination, nor about the witnesses with whom this issue would be raised, the Prosecution could not "adequately prepare these witnesses." The Defence for all three accused responded that Rule 65 ter (F) did not require an accused to set out his or her defence in such detail as the Prosecution suggested and that Idriz Balaj's pre-trial brief, therefore, was in full compliance with the rule. Rule 65 ter (F) states that the pre-trial brief of the Defence should set out the nature of the accused's defence "in general terms." It should also set out the matters with which the accused takes issue in the Prosecutor's pre-trial brief and the reason why the accused takes issue with it. The Chamber considers that the Prosecution has given no foundation for its statement that Idriz Balaj intends to use "the defence of blood feud" in the cross-examination of other witnesses. The Prosecution has merely shown that it constituted only one among several lines of cross-examination in relation to Witness 19. The blood feud issue has been raised in cross-examination just once since Witness 19 by counsel for Ramush Haradinaj. For those, for the parties interested, I refer to transcript pages 3783 to 3785. I continue with the decision. Again, the role of this line of cross-examination was peripheral. Rule 65 ter (F) does not require that the Defence describe the specific lines of questioning it intends to use during cross-examination for each Prosecution witness. Consequently, the Chamber does not consider that the pre-trial brief of Idriz Balaj breaches the mentioned rule. And for these reasons, the Prosecution's motion is denied. This concludes the Chamber's decision. The next decision to be delivered is a decision on the first batch of Prosecution's Rule 92 bis and Rule 92 ter motions. This is a decision on the first batch of Rule 92 bis and 92 ter requests by the Prosecution. The original motion was filed on the 19th of February, 2007, and amended on the 7th of May, 2007. The Defence responded to the original motion on the 1st and the 5th of March, 2007, and to the amended motion on the 21st and 22nd of May, 2007. The Chamber's decision covers the material shown in the form that has already been distributed to the parties. As you will see in the first table appearing in that form, the evidence of three witnesses is being admitted according to Rule 92 bis without cross-examination. Among these three witnesses is one witness whose evidence is only provisionally admitted pending formal attestations. The Chamber has given full consideration to the arguments of the parties, including the Defence's request that the decision be delayed until the Chamber is in a position to determine the alleged cumulative nature of the evidence, where this is applicable. The other three witnesses shown in table 2 of the form you have are being called to appear before the Chamber, and the decision on the admission of their evidence will only be taken on the day they appear in court. The Chamber reminds the Prosecution that the evidence admitted pursuant to Rule 92 bis is public unless a request for protective measures has been received and granted. Until the Prosecution is in a position to affirm that the persons referred to in the first table of the form do not require protective measures, the Chamber will provisionally admit this evidence under seal. The Prosecution is given seven days to inform the Chamber about the security and safety status of these witnesses. Lastly, the Chamber requests the Prosecution to upload the documents shown in the form into e-court, and the registrar to assign exhibit numbers to the in the form and to inform the parties of the exhibit numbers so assigned. This concludes the Chamber's decision on the first batch of 92 bis and 92 ter witnesses. The form will be filed confidentially so that we have clearly on the record what is admitted and what is not admitted. Mr. Re.

utterances.text: The second is Shemsedin Cekaj, who testified on the 16th and 17th of May, 2007, at transcript pages 4378 to 4513, and his Rule 92 ter statement is Exhibit P317. This is the statement of it for the purposes of -- this is the summary of it, sorry, for the purposes of the transcript. And I note that the interpreters all have a copy of the summary I'm reading. Shemsedin Cekaj was born in Irzniq in 1958. After completing high school in Decane, he attended the military academy in Belgrade. After completing the academy in 1981, he served with the JNA in Negotin, Serbia, until he was demobilised in 1992. At the time of his mobilisation [sic], he held the rank of captain first class. From 1992 to early 1998, the witness lived in Peje with his family and worked as a civilian. He first became aware of the KLA appearing in the open when he saw on television three masked and uniformed KLA members attending the funeral of a teacher in Llaushe on November 28th, 1997. The attack involving the Jashari family on the 5th to 7th of March, 1998, in Prekaz first motivated the witness to join the KLA. The witness made the decision to join the KLA after Ramush Haradinaj's family compound was attacked on 24th of March, 1998. After the 24th of March attack, the witness began seeing uniformed KLA soldiers in the streets. Sometime in early 1998, probably before the Prekaz attack, the witness participated in a large public demonstration held at the bus station in Decane. Approximately 30.000 to 40.000 people gathered to show support for the KLA. At that time, according to the witness: "You could smell the war in Kosovo." After the 24th of March attack, the KLA in the villages within the Dukagjin area mobilised and set up defence systems. In mid-May, the witness moved to Irzniq. The day he arrived, he held a meeting with members of the Irzniq KLA staff. At this meeting, he learned that the Irzniq KLA was well-organised. It had already set up trenches, formed units, and trained soldiers. The Irzniq KLA had set up a command structure; however, as everyone in the KLA was a volunteer, this structure was not entirely realised. The total number of KLA soldiers in Irzniq varied between 120 and 170 based on the circumstances. In mid-May the KLA had approximately one weapon for each of the 350 households in the village. At that time, most of the Irzniq KLA soldiers were stationed to the west of Irzniq on the Irzniq-Prilep road. This was a secondary defence position in case the front line at Prilep was penetrated. In June the soldiers moved closer to the front at Prilep and Grdaje to reinforce the front line. The day the witness moved to Irzniq, he attended a large meeting in Gllogjan. Representatives of the village KLA staffs of almost all villages in the Dukagjin area attended; however, the villages on the west side of the road were not able to attend due to the conflict situation. Ramush Haradinaj opened the meeting. Around 25th to 27th of May, there was a Serb offensive into KLA territory from the north and west. Serbian forces got as far as Krushec and Vranoc in the north before withdrawing. They tried to take Prilep and Rastavica in the west but were unsuccessful. On 3rd of June, 1998, Sali Veseli, a former JNA officer who was previously known to the witness, arrived in Kosovo from abroad and went to Gllogjan to meeting with Ramush Haradinaj. A meeting was held at the Gllogjan KLA staff where those present, including Ramush Haradinaj and the witness, briefed Sali Veseli on the situation. It was agreed that Veseli would go to Junik, as this was a strategic location along the supply lines between Albania and the Dukagjin area. Around 24th of June, 1998, the witness attended a meeting in Jablanica at Lahi Brahimaj's house. Present at the meeting were, among others: Ramush Haradinaj, Sali Veseli, Rrustem Tetaj, Skender Rexhahmetaj, Lahi Brahimaj, Nazmi Brahimaj, and Rexhep Selimi. Rexhep Selimi introduced himself as a representative of the General Staff. At this meeting, two candidates for commander of the Dukagjin Plain emerged: Ramush Haradinaj and Lahi Brahimaj. A vote was held and Ramush Haradinaj was elected commander. Lahi Brahimaj became the deputy commander. However, approximately two weeks later, the witness was informed that Ramush had replaced Lahi Brahimaj with Nazmi Brahimaj as his deputy. A group of soldiers arrived from Albania around the end of June 1998. The group was referred to as the FARK, but the witness considered them part of the KLA. The witness knew Tahir Zemaj from his time in the JNA, and the witness was enthusiastic about the arrival of this group of military professionals. In early July, the witness's position within the KLA changed. On 12th of July, 1998, three brigades were formed: The 131st, led by Nazif Ramabaja, based in Baran; the 132nd, led by the witness, based in Bardhaniq/Zhabel; and the 134th, led by Tahir Zemaj, based in Prapaqan. There was another Serbian offensive that began on the morning of 11th of August, 1998. Serbian forces came east from the Decane-Gjakove main road into Baballoq, Rastavica, and Carrabreg. They got as far as Gllogjan, Dubrava, and Shaptej. The witness thought their aim was to control the axis along Gllogjan-Irzniq-Beleg-Decane and to destroy the villages they took along the way. As they moved into the area, the KLA withdrew along with the civilian population to villages inside the area of the fighting, such as Kodrali, Pozhare, Broliq, Lumbardh, and Lluka e Ulet. There was limited KLA resistance to this offensive, which was hampered by a lack of artillery weapons and a shortage of ammunition. The Serbian forces withdrew on the evening of 11th of August, 1998, and re-entered the area on the afternoon of the following day. They returned to the same villages as they had been to the day before, burning the remainder of the houses in these villages. This marked the end of the offensive, and the KLA then returned to its previous positions.

utterances.text: First of all, may I say very considerable progress has been made and is being made, and I don't foresee any significant obstacles to achievement of what Your Honour is requesting. Your Honour may remember that some weeks ago now, I think just before the Easter break, I raised a housekeeping list of issues, one of which was to invite the Prosecution to respond in more detail to the military agreed facts that the Defence has submitted with supporting documentation before the trial began. And Mr. Re's response at that stage was that he had understandably insufficient notice to respond to it at the time, but that is an issue that does need to be taken forward, and the Prosecution's position needs clarification. And may I, therefore, again urge that that be a matter that is moved up the priority list because so far as the comments that Your Honour has just made are concerned and so far as agreement can be reached on those matters, there is obviously scope for reducing oral evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Re, could you inform us on where it approximately is on your priority list, whether it could even move up from there.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: It's up there. We are dealing with it. In relation to getting something together, the form in which we're trying to get it, I'm not telling you what's in it, is in a form in which it could slip into a judgement whatever way a judgement goes and that's the aim of what we're trying to do in the negotiations to come up with a form of wording which is acceptable to both sides, all parties, so that it could be put straight into a judgement as agreed without further qualification.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: It's fine to give it that format, but for the Chamber, most importantly, is agreement between the parties and how to put it in the judgement is a matter which, of course, the Chamber appreciates your concerns, but urges you to focus on results rather than on format. Is there any other matter, procedural matter, to be raised at this moment?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Just one so far as I'm concerned. Following the end of the hearing last Thursday and the conclusion of the post-hearing interparties' meeting about the scheduling for this week, the Prosecution and the Defence had a meeting about witness planning. And yesterday Mr. Re indicated by e-mail the names of two witnesses who are scheduled to give evidence next week. Before I mention their names, I'm looking to see if there's any likely application for protective measures in respect of either of them. I think the witness being dealt with by Mr. Kearney is not a witness for whom there could conceivably be a protective measures application. It's simply Mr. Di Fazio's witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: He says no.

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Without going into details, I simply put the Prosecution and the Trial Chamber on notice that depending upon the content of such statement when it arrives, it may well prove to be a situation in which it is too late to have served the content of fresh evidence to call him next week. It may well give rise to investigations. I've sought clarification from the Prosecution in the past as to whether the statement will reflect the suspect interview in broad terms, and that clarification has not been provided to me; in other words, I was not given that assurance. So I'm simply laying down a marker now that the late service of a new statement from someone who's been interviewed as a suspect is very likely to result in the need for investigations, and I've made that clear for some time to the Prosecution, that late service of his statement followed by a few days' notice of when it is he is to be called is not a situation which I am prepared to willingly acquiesce. A similar statement arises in respect to the other witness from whom notification was given, Jakup Krasniqi, no witness statement from him, although he did testify in the Limaj case and there is a transcript available. I reserve my position in respect of that until I have seen the statement that the Prosecution wishes to serve.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I join specifically to those remarks with regard to those two witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: And I see that Brahimaj Defence is doing the same. Mr. Re, is there any chance that you would provide the Defence with such information that would not cause them to ask for more time?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: The situation is that we are re-interviewing him on the same terms as last time; that is, as a suspect interview. We will disclose the tape of that interview. We should be able to do it tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I indicated to Mr. Re about six or seven weeks ago, when he first suggested to me that this man may be a witness in this case, that as and when we knew what evidence the Prosecution proposed to elicit, we would inevitably need a period for investigation. I think it's extremely unlikely that we will be able to deal with this witness next week.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Mr. Re, first of all, before we continue I'd like to have a redaction made. It seems the first witness you talked about has been assigned a pseudonym from what I understand pre-trial. Therefore, we'll check that, first of all, but, Madam Registrar, that would be --

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I believe it was 37.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes, it was 37, I would agree with that. Yes, Madam Registrar, that would be page 60, line 20 and going on. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I was dealing with that witness. I led Mr. Re into error there, and I apologise for any inconvenience caused to the court. It is a matter that is my responsibility.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. It is a matter of inconvenience for the witness rather than for the Court, Mr. Di Fazio.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: If Mr. Di Fazio has carriage of the witness, one would expect him to know whether he is proposing to make an application for protective measures for his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. But the first concern now is, let's say you would provide the tape by tomorrow, of course, the Defence is urged to see what it can do and we'll perhaps at a later stage have to -- let's not anticipate on what will happen. You could expect the tape tomorrow. Then anything about the second witness mentioned by Mr. Emmerson?

utterances.speaker: MR. RE
utterances.text: Mr. Di Fazio tells me in relation to the first one that there is nothing new to the case that the witness has so far said to him. He will speak to him again this afternoon. And in that sense, we are reasonably confident there is nothing which would require further investigation. In relation to the second witness, I won't be able to inform the Trial Chamber until tomorrow, because we're speaking to him this afternoon, as to whether there is anything additional to his statements which have already been served on the Defence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. You would say for the first witness - we're in private session now – (redacted) -- oh, we're not. I apologise. We should have turned into -- I asked for a redaction but I should have asked to go into private session as well. Well, in relation to the first witness could you make a --

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar. Mr. Guy-Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Yes. There are two issues. One is the remaining issue of the translation of the statement from Mr. Pappas and what is the status of that. We have yet to receive that statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I understand that's to hand. It needs to be dealt with by some procedural matters, and I'm hopeful that we'll be able to forward it on this afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: The second issue deals with a matter that Your Honour raised earlier concerning the corrigendum that had been filed. At this point, I don't know whether or not Your Honours wished for us to respond to that particular document or not. Looking at the remarks made by the Chamber, even if we are to deal with the specific paragraphs sought to be introduced by the Prosecution through the 92 bis procedure, I think the same analysis applies, that was made, which is the investigators cannot at least attest that the witness's statements are true and correct and accurately reflect what the witness would say if examined. So I think we remain in the same position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Well, of course, we'll have to look at these specific paragraphs. We have not done that yet. But corrigendum or not, of course, the Defence has not given an opportunity yet to respond on the corrected now submission. So they could include I think whatever the Defence would like to include; and where the Chamber earlier sought clarification, that was an expression of the concern, the Chamber, by mistake, had. If there's any remaining concern with the Defence, of course, they can deal with it in their response.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: But the Chamber at this moment is not seeking any further clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: Very well. Then we shall do so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please do so. Mr. Emmerson.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to return to the issue of the witness for next week. May I just mention one final matter in closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Private session would do I take it.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: Private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we're back in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. GUY-SMITH
utterances.text: I don't know if it will be of any help to the Chamber or not; however, I'm going back once again to the corrigendum for a moment. The corrigendum as presently constituted I believe, based on my review of the law, should be stricken because what in fact is an entirety of all the statements, and it would be appropriate for the Prosecution to re-file those particular paragraphs that it wishes to have admitted under the 92 bis procedure attached to the statements of those investigators. I don't know whether or not that's something that will make life easier for us or not, but that's one of the matters that I can obviously deal with in the response. It's just that we are catapulting into referrals after referrals after referrals to particular areas, and it may be of more benefit to all the parties involved to have the particular evidence that is under consideration highlighted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. Please address the matter in your response. Any further matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: There is very briefly one further matter. Your Honour's question about the Zyrapi exhibit inconsistency has resulted in an examination of how the situation has come about taking place to my left. And what has been identified is that in the schedule that was attached to the Defence submission, somewhere about two-thirds or three-quarters of the way along, there has been a numerical error which has put out all of the numbers now from that point onwards. As a result, the documents that were identified in the Defence submission do not correspond with the position that the Defence had taken in respect of a small number of documents. And it follows that when Your Honour has ruled in principle in relation to those 99 documents that are agreed and invited Madam Registrar to refer to the Defence pleading for the detail, if she were to do that as it stands today, she would receive erroneous passages from certain passages for the Defence pleading, for which I take responsibility. By tomorrow there will be a corrigendum correcting the position, and I think the anomaly that Your Honour had identified will smooth itself out once that corrigendum is filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: My instruction to the extent Madam Registrar has not already done the job is expended for the time being. We'll wait for your further submissions.

utterances.speaker: MR. EMMERSON
utterances.text: It doesn't in any way change the substance of Your Honour's ruling or the issue between the parties; it's simply a question of numbers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: Yes. If we would continue now that the trial would be at risk to become the comedy of errors or tragedy of errors, whatever way you would look at it. If there's no urgent matter further to be addressed at this moment, we will adjourn until tomorrow, 9.00, in this same courtroom where we'll continue to hear the evidence to be given by Mr. Crosland. We stand adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ORIE
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 23rd day of May, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25
